report.source_text: According to the acute onset of a brainstem lesion, MRI findings and HLA-B51 positivity, we started oral corticosteroid and colchicine therapy after intravenous methylprednisolone administration (1000 mg/day for 3 days) on suspicion of neuro-Behçet’s disease.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A man in his 70s presented with a three-day history of gait disturbance, left hemiparaesthesia, dysarthria, and dysphagia. MRI revealed hyperintense lesions in the brainstem and left caudate nucleus with neuroinflammatory features on MR spectroscopy. Neurological exam showed left-sided sensory deficits, spastic gait, hyperreflexia, and absent plantar reflexes. No mucocutaneous lesions or positive pathergy test were observed on admission, and the patient reported no prior history of oral or genital ulcers. CSF analysis was normal without inflammatory markers or oligoclonal bands. Blood tests were unremarkable, and autoimmune antibodies were negative. HLA typing revealed homozygosity for the B51 allele known to be associated with Behçet's disease. The patient was treated with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral corticosteroid and colchicine therapy. Follow-up MRI after 2 months showed reduction of brain lesions, consistent with response to immunosuppressive treatment. The diagnosis of neuro-Behçet’s disease was made based on the clinical presentation, MRI findings, supportive HLA typing, exclusion of other causes, and treatment response.
